scenario.figure_or_table: Figure 9 (with the Section IV-F setup on PDF page 12)
scenario.description: Thermal-aware redundant-TSV insertion in a 64-core 3D-NoC. Router power is estimated from PARSEC switching activity and energy per bit, and router temperatures are emulated with HotSpot 6.0. The normalized fault rate from Black's model (Eq. 18, coolest area as Tref) drives a grid search of two thresholds (theta1, theta2) that sets 0, 1 or 2 redundant TSVs per group. Figure 9 compares uniform (10:0, 11:1, 11:2) and empirical insertion at target MTTF of 1.5x, 2x and 2.5x MTTF at Tref. The text gives no block coordinates, dimensions or per-block power values, and temperatures are shown only as normalized MTTF or redundancy maps.
scenario.architecture: 4x4x4 3D mesh NoC (64 cores) with a Garnet NoC model in gem5. Routers use IaSiG TSV fault-tolerance modules on the UP and DOWN ports, with 36 TSVs per vertical connection (32 data, 2 spare, 1 sync, 1 parity). Synthesized in NanGate 45 nm with NCSU FreePDK TSV.
scenario.workload: PARSEC benchmarks (switching activities extracted under gem5 3D mesh Garnet NoC simulation)
scenario.operating_point: Reference temperature is the coolest region of the 3D-IC (absolute value not stated). Target MTTF is 1.5x, 2x or 2.5x MTTF at Tref. Absolute powers, temperatures and clock frequency are not given in the text. Black's-model parameters (Ea, J, n) are not given.

original_setup.solver: HotSpot 6.0 emulates the temperature of each router in a 4x4x4 3D-NoC. Router power comes from energy per bit (Synopsys CAD) multiplied by PARSEC switching activities. Black's model (Eq. 18) then converts temperature to a normalized fault rate, with the coolest area as Tref.
original_setup.optimizer: Grid (heuristic) search over two fault-rate thresholds (theta1, theta2). The thresholds set 0, 1 or 2 redundant TSVs per TSV group (Eq. 19) to meet a target MTTF of 1.5x, 2x or 2.5x MTTF at Tref.
original_setup.controller: No thermal controller. The IaSiG on-line TSV fault detection and recovery uses isolation and shift with parity check in hardware. Its parameters are K=32 cycles per test, double-check, and R<=2 redundancies per group of 8 TSVs. It is a reliability mechanism, not a thermal management controller.
original_setup.benchmark: PARSEC benchmarks run in gem5 with a 3D mesh Garnet NoC (64 cores, 4x4x4). Results are compared against uniform redundancy (10:0, 11:1, 11:2) in Figure 9 (PDF page 13).

thermal_observable.unit: normalized MTTF (relative to MTTF at Tref); absolute temperature in K not reported
thermal_observable.location: Per router and per nearby TSV group in the 3D-NoC. Results are shown as the system MTTF and redundancy map in Figure 9, with the coolest region as the reference.
thermal_observable.aggregation: System-level MTTF relative to the target (1.5x, 2x or 2.5x MTTF at Tref). It is derived from per-group normalized fault rates (NFR_T, Eq. 18). No numeric peak or mean temperature is given in the text.

physical_mismatches.reason: The paper gives no block names, x/y positions, widths, heights or per-block power in watts. Figure 9 shows only normalized MTTF and redundancy maps. There is no complete same-scenario floorplan, so none can be extracted, and total power must not be split without a published rule.

The scenario is a 3D stacked NoC (4 layers) with TSV-based vertical links, and HotSpot 6.0 3D layer and interposer configuration is not published. A steady-state 2D Studio model cannot represent the inter-layer thermal coupling or TSV thermal effects that drive the result.

The paper's result is a reliability and MTTF outcome (Black's model, redundancy count), not a temperature field. The thermal solver is only an input to a fault-rate model. Black's-model parameters (Ea, J, n) and the absolute Tref are not given.

The paper's optimizer is a grid search over fault-rate thresholds, and the controller is a hardware TSV fault detector with a WCET of 5,152 cycles. Neither is a thermal controller or cooling policy, and both are workload- and reliability-specific with no counterpart in a Studio thermal setup.

The paper does not state the cooling or package details (heat sink, spreader, TIM) used in HotSpot, and no transient behaviour is reported. The Studio package assumptions cannot be matched to the original.

studio_assumptions: No complete experiment with block geometry and power is available, so the floorplan is empty and no Studio run is justified.

If a Studio run were attempted anyway, its default package, material stack and cooling would replace the HotSpot 6.0 configuration, which the paper does not specify. That run would be a different scenario and not a replication.

The linked reference URLs (NanGate, FreePDK3D45, PARSEC, HotSpot 6.0 report, JPL reliability text) are documentation or library references. They are not evidence that any thermal input file, config, floorplan or power trace exists.

methods.note: The extracted method chain matches the text on PDF pages 9, 12 and 13: PARSEC switching activity and energy per bit give router power, HotSpot 6.0 gives temperature, Black's model (Eq. 17-18) gives the normalized fault rate with the coolest area as Tref, and a grid search over theta1/theta2 (Eq. 19) sets 0, 1 or 2 redundancies. This verifies only the textual description, not a reproducible procedure. The 'TSV thermal effect negligible and not modeled' claim is stronger than the paper's wording on page 14.

assessment.summary: The 2D screening label is not_2d_applicable, and Studio did not run (simulation status: skipped). The gate blocked it because the custom steady experiment has no blocks and no power_w object, so input validity failed. The selected scenario is thermal-aware redundant-TSV insertion in a 4x4x4 (64-core) 3D-NoC (Figure 9, Section IV-F). Its reported outcome is system MTTF relative to a target at Tref, derived from HotSpot 6.0 router temperatures and Black's model. It is not a temperature field. No Studio thermal result exists, and the experiment kind is custom_2d_steady, so there is no transient trace either. comparison_valid is false, and no numerical comparison with the paper's normalized MTTF or redundancy results is made. Nothing here replicates or checks the paper's claim, for example that the no-redundancy 10:0 case falls below 50% of target MTTF. Qualitatively, the paper's logic is that hotter routers have higher fault rates and so receive more redundant TSVs. That is a reliability argument layered on a 3D thermal solve, and it cannot be tested here. A 2D steady Studio model could at best show lateral hotspot sensitivity within one layer. It would not reflect inter-layer coupling, TSV thermal effects, or the Black's-model chain. The gate also lists unresolved evidence-locator, asset-pinning and adversarial-review checks, so the extraction is unverified. The linked references (NanGate, FreePDK3D45, PARSEC, HotSpot 6.0 report, JPL text) are citations, not thermal input files.
limitations: Studio did not run, so there is no simulated thermal output of any kind.

The scenario is a 4-layer 3D stack with TSV vertical links. A steady 2D model cannot represent inter-layer coupling or TSV thermal effects.

The optimizer (grid search over fault-rate thresholds) and the IaSiG hardware TSV fault detector are reliability mechanisms with no thermal-controller counterpart in Studio.
